title: Near-Optimal Regret in Adversarial Kernel Bandits
claim: Restricted special-case losses are simple and localized, whereas general bounded functions in the function class are far richer and multi-modal.
layout: 2 panels side-by-side, shared axes labels, single blue curve each
description: Two side-by-side line plots with identical axis labels: Action x from 0 to 1 on the horizontal axis and Loss on the vertical axis. Each panel has light gray gridlines and one thick blue smooth curve. The left panel shows a rank-one function, a single Gaussian-like bump that peaks at about 1 near x=0.45 and stays flat at 0 elsewhere. The right panel shows a general RKHS-norm bounded function. It is a wiggly curve that starts around 0.4, peaks near 0.6, drops to about -1 near x=0.36, then oscillates with smaller bumps and troughs before rising to about -0.3 at x=1. The eye goes to the contrast between the single sharp peak and the complex multi-extrema curve.
caption: Example of a rank-one function (Left) and a general RKHS-norm bounded function (Right) under the squared exponential kernel, which has exponential eigenvalue decay.
abstract: We study the adversarial kernel bandit problem, in which the loss at each round is induced by an arbitrary bounded element of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). We propose an exponential-weights algorithm built on a regularized importance-weighted loss estimator, together with an explicit correction term that cancels the bias introduced by the regularization. Our main result bounds the regret by $\widetilde{O}\big(\sqrt{T\, d_*(Î»)\,\log|{X}|}\big)$, where $d_*(Î»)$ is a widely-adopted notion of effective dimension that captures the complexity of the kernel. Up to logarithmic factors, this matches the known rate achieved in the related stochastic kernel bandit problem. A notable application is the MatÃ©rn$(Î½,d)$ kernel with smoothness parameter $Î½$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$, for which our bound specializes to $\widetilde{O}\big(T^{(Î½+d)/(2Î½+d)}\big)$, improving over the best-known prior rate of Chatterji et al. [2019] while simultaneously removing the rank-one adversary assumption required by their analysis. Moreover, this rate is the same as the known optimal rate for stochastic kernel bandits, and also matches a lower bound from concurrent work up to a $\log T$ factor.
